$comment: RAGE exposure-db (GCP) — every place customer-controlled credentials/secrets can leak, per service. Each site maps to the RAGE edge it emits (`emits`), the FULL collection recipe (`read`: access_mode/operation/params/response_path/encoding + required_permissions), where it sits (location/location_kind), and what leaks (data_kinds). Vocabulary in exposure-db/vocabulary.json.

sites.description: Access level conditions expose identity members, networks, device posture requirements, and custom CEL expressions.
Service perimeter policy exposes protected resource names, allowed identities, and ingress/egress rules.
Access policy titles are plaintext customer-controlled metadata.
App Engine version environment variables are persisted and returned in version configuration.
Version beta settings are an arbitrary plaintext map and can accumulate credentials or connection details.
Deployed application files can contain hard-coded credentials and configuration secrets.
App Engine application create and patch requests can carry an input-only IAP OAuth client secret.
An App Engine authorized-certificate request can carry an unencrypted PEM private key that is input-only after creation.
Downloaded packages, archives, and container layers may contain hard-coded secrets or sensitive source artifacts.
Repository descriptions and labels are plaintext metadata.
Package annotations are arbitrary plaintext metadata.
Version annotations are arbitrary plaintext metadata.
Batch task environment variables are returned in job configuration.
Inline Batch runnable scripts can hard-code credentials or sensitive shell content.
Container commands and option strings can contain inline secrets.
A private-registry password supplied as plaintext is retained in the Batch job and exposed to users who can view the job or its logs.
Batch status descriptions can echo execution errors and user-controlled values.
BigQuery table rows may contain credentials, tokens, PII, or arbitrary sensitive data.
Completed query results may contain sensitive values selected from one or more sources.
Saved job configuration retains SQL text and literal query parameters that may contain secrets or PII.
Routine SQL or source code can contain hard-coded credentials and sensitive literals.
Table descriptions and labels are plaintext metadata.
Dataset descriptions and labels are plaintext metadata.
Row access policy predicates can contain sensitive literals and schema identifiers.
Bigtable cells can store arbitrary credentials and customer data.
Bigtable instance labels are plaintext metadata.
Column-family names and garbage-collection policies can disclose schema and retention details.
Certificate Manager exposes managed public certificate material and chain metadata.
Self-managed certificate create and update requests carry the PEM private key as an input-only field.

Certificate Authority Service returns issued certificate PEM and chain data.
Certificate labels are plaintext metadata.
Cloud Armor CEL expressions can include sensitive hostnames, paths, identifiers, or literal values.
Cloud Armor header actions may inject literal credentials or sensitive values into requests.
Security-policy rule descriptions are plaintext customer-controlled metadata.
Asset search aggregates free-form descriptions, labels, and service-specific additional attributes.
IAM policy analysis exposes identities, group expansion, roles, permissions, and access-control paths.
Asset feed resource selectors, CEL conditions, and destination configuration are plaintext.
Exported asset inventory can include resource metadata, IAM policies, and service-specific sensitive fields in Cloud Storage.
Build-step environment entries persist literal name/value strings in the build record.
Build command arguments may contain inline tokens, passwords, or signed URLs.
User-defined substitutions are plaintext build configuration and may be misused for secrets.
A trigger's inline build template can embed credentials in commands, environment values, and substitutions.

Cloud Functions configuration returns this customer-controlled plaintext field to authorized readers.

Custom metadata on Container Registry backing objects is plaintext.
Cloud Storage object bodies may contain any uploaded credential, source artifact, backup, or customer data.
Object custom metadata is plaintext and may contain credentials or sensitive identifiers.
Bucket labels are plaintext metadata.
Cloud Storage returns the new HMAC secret only in the key-creation response.
Bucket IAM policies expose principal identifiers and conditional expressions.
A Cloud Storage object-notification channel can carry an arbitrary verification token that is delivered with every notification.
Kubernetes Secrets are merely base64-encoded in the API and commonly hold workload credentials.
ConfigMaps are plaintext and are frequently misused for passwords, API keys, and application configuration.
Pod templates can persist literal credentials in environment variable values.
Container command and argument arrays may contain inline secrets.
Legacy cluster basic-auth and client-certificate credentials may be returned when those deprecated mechanisms remain configured.
GKE resource labels are plaintext metadata.
IAM Conditions are plaintext expressions and descriptions in which operators may embed sensitive identifiers or values.
Policy members disclose user, group, domain, service-account, and federated-principal identifiers.
Custom-role titles and descriptions are customer-controlled plaintext metadata.
Deny policies disclose principal identifiers and exceptions.
Deny-rule CEL expressions and descriptions can contain sensitive names or literals.
IAP IAM policies disclose identities allowed to reach protected applications.
IAP policy conditions are plaintext expressions and customer-authored descriptions.
The IAP OAuth client resource returns its client secret to callers with the dedicated get-with-secret permission.
IAP access settings can carry application and workforce OAuth client secrets as input-only plaintext fields.
Cloud KMS decrypt returns plaintext bytes to the caller.
Raw RSA decryption returns plaintext bytes to the caller.
An asymmetric signature can authenticate attacker-controlled content without revealing the private key.
A generated MAC can authenticate attacker-controlled data without exposing key material.
KEM decapsulation returns the derived shared secret as base64-encoded bytes.
CryptoKey labels are plaintext metadata.
URL-map header actions can persist literal Authorization, API-key, cookie, or other sensitive header values.
Backend custom headers may contain literal credentials or sensitive routing values.
An IAP OAuth client secret is a write-only backend-service input and can leak through IaC state or request logging.

The SSL certificate resource returns PEM certificate material and subject metadata.
Application, platform, and audit log payloads can contain request bodies, headers, tokens, stack traces, or customer records.

Metric samples and labels can carry user IDs, request attributes, or other sensitive telemetry.
Alert documentation, queries, filters, and labels are plaintext and may contain internal runbook details or URLs.
Dashboard widgets, filters, queries, text blocks, and labels may expose sensitive operational details.
Legacy uptime-check basic-auth configuration includes a username and password field readable through the config API.
Uptime-check custom headers and paths can contain API keys, cookies, or signed query data.
NCC hub descriptions and labels are plaintext metadata.
NCC spoke descriptions and labels are plaintext metadata.
Spoke linkage fields disclose internal topology and resource identifiers.
The service connection token resource returns the token used to establish producer-consumer connectivity.
The service connection map returns its authentication token to authorized readers.
Organization Policy allow and deny lists may expose project, resource, network, or domain identifiers.
Organization Policy CEL conditions and descriptions are plaintext configuration.
